result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.shortest_path_length()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get the length of the shortest path between two nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L45569-L45648){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.shortest_path_length( source, target, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Shortest path length](/assets/graphs/shortest-path-length.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The directed weighted graph with three routes from A to F, costing 4, 6, and 5. On a weighted graph the distance is the cheapest total weight, so the route A, B, C, F is drawn in the accent color and the card reads 1 + 2 + 1 = 4.0; on the unweighted graph the same call counts hops and returns 2." width="100%"} Returns the distance from `source=` to `target=` without building the path itself. On an unweighted graph (the default) the distance is the number of hops, returned as an `int`. On a weighted graph (`Graph(weighted=True)`) it is the lowest total edge weight, found with Dijkstra's algorithm, returned as a `float`; edges without a weight count as `1.0`. This is the same notion of "shortest" that `shortest_path()` uses, so the two always agree. Directed graphs are followed in edge direction. A node is at distance `0` from itself. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The starting node, as an integer ID or a string label. [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The destination node, as an integer ID or a string label. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [int | float | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The shortest-path distance, or `None` if `target=` cannot be reached from `source=`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a label does not exist in the graph, or a weighted graph has a negative edge weight (use `bellman_ford_shortest_path()` for those). ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} In this directed graph the fewest-hops route from A to F takes two hops, but the cheapest route by weight is the three-hop path through B and C: ::: {#0f26a4aa .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec edges = [ ("A", "B", 1.0), ("B", "C", 2.0), ("C", "F", 1.0), ("A", "D", 3.0), ("D", "F", 3.0), ] hops = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_nodes(list("ABCDF")).add_edges(edges) weights = ec.Graph(directed=True, weighted=True).add_nodes(list("ABCDF")).add_edges(edges) hops.shortest_path_length("A", "F"), weights.shortest_path_length("A", "F") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (2, 4.0) ``` ::: ::: Edges only run forward, so there is no way back from F to A: ::: {#931d8d22 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} hops.shortest_path_length("F", "A") is None ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` True ``` ::: :::
